evidence_quotes.quote: Our focus is on the seventh round, conducted in 34 African countries in 2016–2018.
In Column 2, we introduce the regional incidence of utilities corruption.
that utilities corruption is a meaningful barrier to water access for households in Africa on average.
utilities corruption is only associated with access to water in areas with a piped water
By contrast, we do not find that corruption in other contexts predicts access to water.

raw_response.headline_result_summary: Using Afrobarometer Round 7 household survey data across 34 African countries (N = 44,778), Breen and Gillanders (2024) find that a higher regional incidence of bribery/corruption in the utilities sector (water, sanitation, or electricity) is negatively associated with household access to enough clean water (probit marginal effect = -0.16, SE = 0.073, p < 0.05 in Table 2 Col 3; -0.15, SE = 0.073, p < 0.05 in Col 2). This negative association holds only in enumeration areas with a piped water system (ME = -0.14, SE = 0.045, p < 0.01, N = 24,511) and is null in areas without piped water (ME = -0.12, SE = 0.158, N = 20,267), and is robust in ordered probit models across shortage frequencies (ME on 'Never' lacking clean water = -0.4272, SE = 0.1860, p < 0.05 in Table 3), though attenuated to p < 0.10 when controlling for non-utility regional corruption (ME = -0.13, SE = 0.073 in Table 2 Col 5) and contradicted in pre-CAPI Afrobarometer rounds (null in Round 5; positive in Round 6 and pooled Rounds 5–7). Individual household bribery is not significantly associated with having enough clean water in main models (ME = -0.00, SE = 0.006 in Table 2 Col 3), although individual bribe-payers are more likely to have a nominal water source inside their house or compound (ME = +0.06, SE = 0.018, p < 0.01 in Table 4 Col 1). Coded in the direction of the authors' exposure (higher corruption), regional utilities corruption is unfavorable to household water access (equivalently, lower corruption / higher institutional integrity is favorable to access).
raw_response.specification_or_coding_pitfalls:
1. EXPOSURE POLARITY (CORRUPTION VS. ANTI-CORRUPTION/GOVERNANCE QUALITY): The focal exposure (`Regional incidence of utility corruption`) is scaled so higher values = MORE corruption (worse governance). Its raw sign on `Access` is negative (-0.16, p < 0.05), meaning corruption is `unfavorable_to_access`. If a review synthesis orients institutional governance exposures positively (i.e., control of corruption / regulatory integrity -> access), the substantive direction must be flipped to `favorable_to_access` (better governance/less corruption -> better access).
2. OUTCOME POLARITY FLIP BETWEEN TABLE 2 AND TABLE 3: In Table 2, `Access = 1` means NOT always going without clean water (higher = BETTER access; raw sign = -0.16**). In Table 3 (ordered probit), columns 2–5 (`Just once or twice` through `Always` going without water) measure water deprivation frequency (higher = WORSE access; raw signs are positive, e.g., +0.1095** for `Always`), whereas column 1 (`Never` going without water) measures uninterrupted access (higher = BETTER access; raw sign = -0.4272**). All columns in Table 3 show the same substantive direction (regional corruption worsens access).
3. REGIONAL CORRUPTION VS. INDIVIDUAL BRIBERY & RELIABILITY VS. NOMINAL CONNECTION: Regional utility corruption reduces clean water adequacy (`Access` ME = -0.16**) and is null on source location (`Homesource` ME = -0.26, SE = 0.202), whereas individual household bribery is null on clean water adequacy (`Access` ME = -0.00, SE = 0.006; though positive in leave-one-out Appendix Table A5 per Endnote 5) but positive on having an in-home/compound source (`Homesource` ME = +0.06***). Confusing individual bribery or `Homesource` with regional corruption on `Access` will invert or nullify the result.
4. ATTENUATION AND CROSS-ROUND INSTABILITY: Controlling for non-utility regional corruption attenuates regional utility corruption to p < 0.10 (-0.13*, SE = 0.073, Table 2 Col 5), and earlier Afrobarometer surveys show null (Round 5) or opposite/positive (Round 6 and pooled Rounds 5–7) associations (p. 12).
5. COMPOSITE UTILITIES EXPOSURE: The bribery survey item covers water, sanitation, OR electricity services jointly rather than water services alone.
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional multi-country observational household survey study estimating binary probit and ordered probit models with country fixed effects and region-clustered standard errors (Afrobarometer Round 7, 2016–2018)
raw_response.unit_and_sample_size: Individual respondents / households nested within subnational regions across 34 African countries. Primary analytic sample N = 44,778 (models with individual bribery, Tables 1, 2 Cols 1 & 3, Table 3) and N = 44,887 (models without individual bribery, Table 2 Cols 2, 4, 5); subsamples N = 24,511 (piped water areas, Table 2 Col 7) and N = 20,267 (non-piped areas, Table 2 Col 6); water source location models N = 44,546 (Table 4).
